subject: chemistry
title: Planning a synthesis
summary: Retrosynthetic analysis, functional group interconversions, C–C bond formation, an introduction to protecting groups, and calculating overall yields over multiple steps.
body:
Synthesis is the art of making a target molecule from simpler, available starting materials — the everyday work of chemists who make medicines, agricultural chemicals and materials. Rather than guessing forwards, synthetic chemists work backwards from the target, using the reactions they know as tools. This lesson shows you how to plan a synthesis logically, choose reagents, protect groups that would get in the way, and calculate the yield of a multistep route.

## Think of it like this

### Retrosynthesis is like working out a recipe from a dish you tasted

Imagine eating an amazing dish at a restaurant and trying to cook it at home. You work backwards: "this sauce is probably made from tomatoes and garlic… those I can buy at the supermarket." **Retrosynthesis** is the same: you start from the **target molecule** and make imaginary **disconnections**, asking "what could this be made from?" Each disconnection gives two imaginary pieces called **synthons**, and then you find the real "supermarket ingredients" that behave like them — the **synthetic equivalents**, such as a Grignard reagent (RMgBr) for an R⁻ synthon and an aldehyde or ketone for the carbonyl cation.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* when cooking you can often swap ingredients or guess, but every disconnection in chemistry must match a real reaction you can actually run forwards, and synthons such as R⁻ never exist on their own.

### Protecting groups are like masking tape when you paint a room

If you paint a wall but don't want paint on the light switch, you cover the switch with masking tape, paint, then peel the tape off. A **protecting group** does exactly this: you temporarily convert a group that would get in the way into something unreactive, carry out the reaction you want elsewhere in the molecule, then remove it. For example, an aldehyde or ketone can be "taped over" as a cyclic **acetal**, which survives Grignard reagents and LiAlH₄, and is "peeled off" later with aqueous acid.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* masking tape is quick, but each protecting group adds two whole reaction steps (on and off), each with its own yield losses — so chemists only protect a group when no **chemoselective** reagent can do the job.

### A convergent synthesis is like splitting up a group assignment

If four friends each write one section of an assignment at the same time and then put it together at the end, it's finished much faster than if one person did every section in a row. A **convergent synthesis** makes separate fragments in parallel and joins them near the end, while a **linear synthesis** does every step one after another. Because the overall yield is the product of the step yields (six steps at 90% give only 53%), the convergent route usually wastes less material — its overall yield depends on the longest linear sequence, not the total number of steps.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* in a group assignment a weak section only lowers the mark a little, but in synthesis a low-yield step reduces the amount of material available for every later step.

### In real life

Every medicine made in a factory, from common pain relievers to new cancer drugs, is produced by a planned synthesis, and chemists choose routes with fewer steps, higher yields and better **atom economy** to cut cost and waste. The same thinking is used to make agricultural chemicals and new materials.

## Key ideas

### Retrosynthetic analysis

**Retrosynthesis** (retrosynthetic analysis) means working backwards from the **target molecule** to simpler precursors, one step at a time, until you reach readily available starting materials. Each backwards step is called a **disconnection** — an imaginary breaking of a bond that corresponds to a real reaction you could run forwards. It is written with an open "retrosynthetic arrow" (⇒), which means "could be made from".

When you disconnect a bond, you imagine it splitting into two charged fragments called **synthons** — one nucleophilic, one electrophilic. Each synthon must then be matched to a real reagent, its **synthetic equivalent**. For example, disconnecting a C–C bond next to an alcohol carbon gives a carbanion synthon (R⁻) and a cation synthon at the former carbonyl carbon. The real reagents are a Grignard reagent (RMgBr) and an aldehyde or ketone.

Good disconnections:

- break bonds *next to* functional groups, because that is where reactions happen;
- form C–C bonds near the middle of the molecule, giving two fragments of similar size;
- lead to simple, cheap starting materials;
- avoid steps where other groups in the molecule would react too.

### Functional group interconversions

A **functional group interconversion (FGI)** changes one functional group into another without changing the carbon skeleton. FGIs are often needed before or after a C–C bond-forming step. The core first-year toolkit:

| From | To | Typical reagent(s) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alkene | Alcohol | H₂O, H₃PO₄ catalyst, heat | Markovnikov alcohol |
| Alkene | Haloalkane | HBr | Markovnikov product |
| Alkene | Alkane | H₂, Pd or Ni catalyst | Addition of H₂ |
| Alcohol | Alkene | conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄, heat | Elimination; Zaitsev product |
| Haloalkane | Alcohol | NaOH(aq), heat | SN2 for 1° |
| Haloalkane | Nitrile | KCN in ethanol | Adds one carbon |
| Haloalkane | Amine | excess NH₃ | Excess limits further alkylation |
| 1° alcohol | Aldehyde | PCC | Stops at the aldehyde |
| 1° alcohol | Carboxylic acid | K₂Cr₂O₇ / H₂SO₄ or KMnO₄ / H⁺, reflux | Full oxidation |
| 2° alcohol | Ketone | K₂Cr₂O₇ / H₂SO₄ or PCC | 3° alcohols do not oxidise |
| Aldehyde / ketone | Alcohol | NaBH₄, then H₃O⁺ | Reduction |
| Ester / acid | 1° alcohol | LiAlH₄, then H₃O⁺ | NaBH₄ is too weak |
| Nitrile | Carboxylic acid | H₃O⁺, heat | Hydrolysis |
| Nitrile | 1° amine | LiAlH₄, then H₃O⁺ | Reduction |
| Carboxylic acid + alcohol | Ester | conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat | Condensation; reversible |
| Acid chloride + amine | Amide | Room temperature | Fast and irreversible |

### Carbon–carbon bond formation

Most targets need the carbon skeleton to be built, not just modified. First-year C–C bond-forming reactions include:

- **Haloalkane + cyanide** → nitrile (one extra carbon), which can become an acid or amine.
- **Grignard reagent + carbonyl compound** → alcohol. RMgBr is made from RBr and magnesium in dry ether. With methanal it gives a 1° alcohol, with other aldehydes a 2° alcohol, with ketones a 3° alcohol, and with CO₂ a carboxylic acid. Grignard reagents are destroyed by water, alcohols and acids (they are strong bases), so they need dry conditions and no acidic O–H or N–H groups in the molecule.
- **Cyanohydrin formation** (HCN + aldehyde or ketone) adds one carbon and gives an OH and CN on the same carbon.

### Chemoselectivity and protecting groups

**Chemoselectivity** is the preference of a reagent for one functional group over another. NaBH₄, for example, reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters or carboxylic acids, so it can reduce a ketone selectively in a molecule that also contains an ester.

When no reagent is selective enough, you use a **protecting group**: a temporary modification that makes a group unreactive, which is removed later. A good protecting group goes on easily, survives the conditions you need, and comes off cleanly without affecting the rest of the molecule. Common introductory examples:

- **Acetals** protect aldehydes and ketones. Reacting the carbonyl with ethane-1,2-diol and an acid catalyst forms a cyclic acetal, which is stable to bases, nucleophiles, Grignard reagents, NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄. Aqueous acid removes it.
- **Silyl ethers** (e.g. a tert-butyldimethylsilyl, TBS, ether) protect alcohols. They are stable to bases and many oxidising and reducing agents, and are removed by fluoride ion.
- **Esters** can protect alcohols, removed by hydrolysis.

Each protecting group adds two steps (on and off), which lowers the overall yield, so use them only when needed.

### Yields over multiple steps

The **percentage yield** of a single step is

% yield = (actual amount of product / theoretical amount) × 100%

For a **linear synthesis** (A → B → C → … in sequence), the overall yield is the *product* of the step yields expressed as decimals:

overall yield = y₁ × y₂ × y₃ × …

This falls quickly: six steps at 90% each give 0.90⁶ = 0.53, only 53%. That is why chemists value short routes and prefer **convergent syntheses**, in which separate fragments are made in parallel and joined near the end. The overall yield then depends on the longest linear sequence, which is shorter than the total number of steps.

**Atom economy** is a separate measure: the percentage of the mass of all reactants that ends up in the desired product. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy; substitutions and eliminations produce by-products and have lower atom economy.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: A two-step route with a yield calculation

Plan a synthesis of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, from bromoethane, and calculate the mass of product from 10.0 g of bromoethane if the steps give 85% and 75% yields.

Retrosynthesis:

1. Propanoic acid has three carbons; bromoethane has two. A carbon must be added.
2. A carboxylic acid ⇒ a nitrile (FGI by hydrolysis). Propanoic acid ⇒ CH₃CH₂CN.
3. A nitrile ⇒ a haloalkane + cyanide (C–C disconnection). CH₃CH₂CN ⇒ CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻.

Forward route:

`CH₃CH₂Br(l) + KCN(ethanol) → CH₃CH₂CN(l) + KBr(s)`   (step 1, SN2, 85%)

`CH₃CH₂CN(l) + 2H₂O(l) + H⁺(aq) → CH₃CH₂COOH(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq)`   (step 2, acid hydrolysis, 75%)

Yield calculation:

1. n(CH₃CH₂Br) = m/M = 10.0 g / 108.96 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0918 mol
2. Both steps are 1:1, so theoretical n(acid) = 0.0918 mol.
3. Overall yield = 0.85 × 0.75 = 0.6375 (63.75%)
4. Actual n(acid) = 0.0918 × 0.6375 = 0.0585 mol
5. m = nM = 0.0585 mol × 74.08 g mol⁻¹ = **4.33 g**

### Example 2: Grignard disconnection of a tertiary alcohol

Plan a synthesis of 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃.

1. The target is a 3° alcohol, which suggests Grignard reagent + ketone.
2. Disconnect a C–C bond to the alcohol carbon. There are two sensible choices:
   - Break the ethyl bond: ⇒ propanone, (CH₃)₂C=O, + CH₃CH₂MgBr.
   - Break a methyl bond: ⇒ butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, + CH₃MgBr.
3. Both work. Choosing propanone + ethylmagnesium bromide uses two very common starting materials.
4. Forward: make CH₃CH₂MgBr from bromoethane and Mg in dry ether; add propanone; then add dilute acid to protonate the alkoxide and give the alcohol.

### Example 3: Using a protecting group

You want to convert ethyl 4-oxopentanoate, CH₃COCH₂CH₂COOCH₂CH₃, into 5-hydroxypentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₂OH — that is, reduce the ester to an alcohol but keep the ketone.

1. Problem: LiAlH₄ is needed to reduce the ester, but it would also reduce the ketone. NaBH₄ would reduce only the ketone — the opposite of what we want.
2. Step 1 (protect): ethane-1,2-diol with an acid catalyst converts the ketone into a cyclic acetal.
3. Step 2 (react): LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then a careful workup, reduces the ester to CH₂OH; the acetal is unaffected.
4. Step 3 (deprotect): aqueous acid hydrolyses the acetal back to the ketone.
5. If the steps give 90%, 80% and 90%, the overall yield is 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.648, or **65%**.

## Common mistakes

- Multiplying percentage yields as whole numbers (85 × 75) or adding them, instead of multiplying decimals.
- Proposing a Grignard reaction on a molecule that has an O–H, N–H or C=O group elsewhere that would destroy or react with the reagent.
- Forgetting to count carbons: if the target has more carbons than the starting material, you need a C–C bond-forming step.
- Using NaBH₄ to reduce esters or carboxylic acids — it is not strong enough; LiAlH₄ is needed.
- Oxidising a 1° alcohol with acidified dichromate under reflux and expecting an aldehyde; reflux takes it to the carboxylic acid.

## Exam tips

- Show your retrosynthesis with ⇒ arrows and name each disconnection or FGI, then write the forward route with reagents and conditions for every step.
- Always state conditions (e.g. "dry ether", "reflux", "acid catalyst"); marks are often lost for reagents with no conditions.
- In yield questions, write the overall yield as a product of decimals before converting to mass, and carry extra figures until the end.
- If a step would affect another group, say so and propose a protecting group or a more selective reagent.

## Tips to remember

- **Retrosynthesis is like planning a road trip from the destination back.** Start at the target, ask "what could this be made from?" (⇒), and keep going until you reach cheap starting materials — then drive the route forwards with reagents and conditions.
- **"Disconnect next to the functional group, near the middle."** Bonds next to functional groups are where reactions happen, and splitting near the middle gives two similar-sized, simpler fragments.
- **Count carbons first.** If the target has more carbons than the starting material, you need a C–C bond-forming step: cyanide (+1 C), cyanohydrin (+1 C) or a Grignard reagent. Grignard products: methanal → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3° alcohol, CO₂ → carboxylic acid.
- **Grignards hate water — "keep it dry, keep it O–H-free."** They are strong bases, so dry ether is essential and no acidic O–H or N–H can be present in the molecule.
- **NaBH₄ is the gentle reducer, LiAlH₄ the heavy hitter.** NaBH₄ reduces only aldehydes and ketones; esters, acids and nitriles need LiAlH₄. Similarly PCC stops a 1° alcohol at the aldehyde, while acidified dichromate under reflux goes all the way to the carboxylic acid.
- **Yields multiply as decimals.** Six steps at 90% give 0.90⁶ = 0.53 (53%) — the leaky-bucket effect: a little spills at every step. Each protecting group adds two steps (on and off), so use one only when needed, and prefer short or convergent routes.

## Key terms

- **Target molecule** — the compound a synthesis aims to make.
- **Retrosynthesis** — working backwards from the target to simpler starting materials.
- **Disconnection** — imaginary bond break that corresponds to a known forward reaction.
- **Synthon** — idealised charged fragment from a disconnection.
- **Synthetic equivalent** — real reagent that behaves like a synthon.
- **Functional group interconversion (FGI)** — changing one functional group into another without changing the skeleton.
- **Grignard reagent** — RMgBr, a strongly nucleophilic and basic carbon source used to make C–C bonds.
- **Chemoselectivity** — a reagent's preference for one functional group over another.
- **Protecting group** — temporary modification that makes a group unreactive during another step.
- **Acetal** — protected form of an aldehyde or ketone, stable to base and removed by aqueous acid.
- **Linear synthesis** — steps carried out one after another on a single chain of intermediates.
- **Convergent synthesis** — fragments made separately and joined late in the route.
- **Atom economy** — percentage of reactant mass that ends up in the desired product.

## Summary

- Plan syntheses backwards with retrosynthesis: disconnect bonds next to functional groups and match synthons to real reagents.
- FGIs (oxidation, reduction, substitution, elimination, addition, hydrolysis) adjust functional groups; C–C bond-forming steps (cyanide, Grignard) build the skeleton.
- Choose chemoselective reagents where possible; otherwise protect, react, then deprotect.
- Overall yield of a linear synthesis is the product of step yields as decimals; short and convergent routes give better overall yields.
- Always give reagents and conditions, and check that no other group in the molecule interferes.

questions.prompt: In retrosynthetic analysis, what does the open arrow (⇒) mean?

options.B: The target could be made from the species on the right
options.C: The reaction proceeds via a radical mechanism

questions.explanation: The retrosynthetic arrow means 'could be made from', pointing from the target back towards its precursors. Option A confuses it with the equilibrium arrow ⇌, which is a different symbol with a different meaning.

questions.prompt: Which reagent will reduce the ketone in a molecule that also contains an ester, while leaving the ester untouched?
questions.explanation: NaBH₄ is a mild hydride donor that reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters — a chemoselective choice. Option A is tempting because LiAlH₄ certainly reduces ketones, but it also reduces esters, so it is not selective. Dichromate is an oxidant, not a reductant.

questions.prompt: A linear synthesis has five steps, each with an 80% yield. What is the overall yield?
questions.explanation: Overall yield = 0.80⁵ = 0.328, or 33%. Option B assumes the yield stays the same over all steps; option C adds the yields; option D divides 80% by 5. The overall yield is always the product of the step yields as decimals.

questions.prompt: Why is a protecting group needed if you want to react CH₃MgBr with the ketone group of 4-hydroxybutan-2-one, HOCH₂CH₂COCH₃?

options.A: The ketone is too unreactive towards Grignard reagents
options.B: The OH group would be oxidised by the Grignard reagent
options.C: The acidic O–H proton would destroy the Grignard reagent, so the OH must be protected first
options.D: The Grignard reagent would add to the OH group to form an ether

questions.explanation: Grignard reagents are strong bases and are protonated by O–H groups, giving methane and consuming the reagent. Protecting the alcohol (e.g. as a silyl ether) prevents this. Option D is tempting but wrong: the reaction with an O–H is acid–base, not addition to form an ether.

questions.prompt: Which disconnection and reagents would give butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: Disconnecting the C2–C3 bond gives ethanal (CH₃CHO) and an ethyl Grignard; their reaction forms the secondary alcohol CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. Option B gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol. Option C gives butan-1-ol, and option D also gives butan-1-ol.

questions.prompt: Ethanol must be converted into propanoic acid. Which statement is correct about the route?

options.A: Oxidise ethanol with acidified dichromate under reflux
options.B: Convert ethanol to bromoethane, react with KCN, then hydrolyse the nitrile with acid
options.C: React ethanol with methanol and conc. H₂SO₄
options.D: Dehydrate ethanol to ethene, then hydrate with H₂O/H₃PO₄

questions.explanation: Propanoic acid has three carbons and ethanol has two, so a C–C bond must be formed. Bromoethane + cyanide adds one carbon, and hydrolysis turns the nitrile into the acid. Option A is tempting, but oxidation gives ethanoic acid (two carbons). Option C makes an ether or ester, not an acid; option D just returns ethanol.

questions.prompt: Why are convergent syntheses generally preferred over linear syntheses of the same total number of steps?

options.A: They avoid the use of protecting groups
options.C: Every step in a convergent synthesis has a higher yield
options.D: The overall yield depends on the longest linear sequence, which is shorter

questions.explanation: In a convergent route, fragments are made in parallel, so fewer yield losses accumulate on the main chain. Option C is tempting, but individual step yields are not necessarily higher — the advantage comes from fewer steps in sequence.

questions.prompt: A three-step synthesis converts 0.200 mol of starting material into product (all steps 1:1) with step yields of 90%, 70% and 85%. What amount of product is obtained?
questions.explanation: Overall yield = 0.90 × 0.70 × 0.85 = 0.5355. Product = 0.200 × 0.5355 = 0.107 mol. Option A uses the mean step yield (81.7%) instead of the product. Option D uses only the lowest step yield (70%).
